title: Concrete σ Values via native_decide
content: Thirteen specific values of σ are verified computationally using `native_decide`, which compiles and runs code at type-check time. These include σ(6)=12 (perfect number check) and σ(28)=56 (second perfect number). The pattern σ(p) = p+1 for primes is visible in σ(2)=3, σ(3)=4, σ(5)=6, σ(7)=8. Computational verification with `native_decide` provides certainty about specific values while general theorems (proved later) provide structural understanding.

title: General σ(p) = p+1 for All Primes
content: The general theorem sigma_prime proves σ(p) = p+1 for any prime p, not just specific values. The proof uses `sigma_apply_prime_pow hp` with k=1 to get σ(p) = Σ_{j=0}^{1} p^j = 1 + p, then simplifies with `simp [pow_one, Finset.sum_range_succ]` and closes with `linarith`. This is the structural key: primes have exactly two divisors (1 and p), so σ = 1 + p.
mathContext:
$$\sigma(p) = p + 1 \text{ for all primes } p$$
Proof: divisors of $p$ are $\{1, p\}$ only. From `sigma_apply_prime_pow`: $\sigma(p^1) = \sum_{j=0}^{1} p^j = 1 + p$.

title: Number Classification: Deficient, Perfect, Abundant
content: Three classification predicates are defined in terms of σ(n) vs 2n: IsDeficient (σ(n) < 2n), IsPerfect (σ(n) = 2n), IsAbundant (σ(n) > 2n). Perfect numbers satisfy σ(n) = 2n because σ(n) = n + s(n) where s(n) is the sum of proper divisors, so σ(n) = 2n means s(n) = n. The first three perfect numbers 6, 28, 496 are all verified by native_decide. All primes are deficient since σ(p) = p+1 < 2p.
mathContext:
$$\text{Deficient}: \sigma(n) < 2n, \quad \text{Perfect}: \sigma(n) = 2n, \quad \text{Abundant}: \sigma(n) > 2n$$
$$\sigma(n) = n + s(n) \text{ where } s(n) = \sum_{\substack{d|n \\ d < n}} d$$
Perfect $\Leftrightarrow s(n) = n$.

title: Classification is Exhaustive and Exclusive via omega
content: The three categories (deficient, perfect, abundant) partition the positive integers. Exhaustiveness — every n falls into at least one — follows by trichotomy of natural number comparison: σ(n) < 2n ∨ σ(n) = 2n ∨ σ(n) > 2n, closed by `omega`. Exclusivity of each pair (deficient ∧ perfect → contradiction, etc.) also follows by linear arithmetic after unfolding definitions. The `omega` tactic handles all four theorems elegantly, demonstrating that classification logic reduces entirely to natural number arithmetic.
mathContext:
$$\forall n,\; \text{IsDeficient}(n) \vee \text{IsPerfect}(n) \vee \text{IsAbundant}(n)$$
and the three are pairwise mutually exclusive. Proof by $\lt, =, >$ trichotomy of $\sigma(n)$ vs $2n$.

title: Amicable Pairs (220,284) and (1184,1210) Formally Verified
content: Two numbers m and n are amicable if σ(m) - m = n and σ(n) - n = m (each is the sum of proper divisors of the other), equivalently σ(m) = σ(n) = m + n. The pair (220, 284) was known to the Pythagoreans (~300 BCE): σ(220) = 504 = 220 + 284. The pair (1184, 1210) was discovered by 16-year-old Niccolò Paganini in 1866, remarkably overlooked by Euler. Both are verified by native_decide for σ values, then omega for the subtraction arithmetic. Over 1.2 billion amicable pairs are known computationally.

title: General Bound: σ(n) > n for n > 1 via Finset Summation
content: The general bound σ(n) > n for all n > 1 is proved by exhibiting two distinct divisors: 1 and n itself. The proof constructs the subset {1, n} ⊆ n.divisors using `Nat.mem_divisors`, shows these are distinct (1 ≠ n since n > 1), then uses `Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg` and `Finset.sum_pair` to bound σ(n) ≥ 1 + n > n. This is an elegant example of bounding a Finset sum by restricting to a chosen subset.
mathContext:
$$\sigma(n) = \sum_{d|n} d \geq 1 + n > n \quad \text{for } n > 1$$
Proof: $\{1, n\} \subseteq \text{divisors}(n)$, both distinct, so $\sigma(n) \geq \sum_{d \in \{1,n\}} d = 1 + n > n$.

title: Multiplicativity: σ(mn) = σ(m)σ(n) for Coprime Inputs
content: The key structural theorem: σ is a multiplicative arithmetic function. `sigma_multiplicative` is a one-liner invoking Mathlib's `isMultiplicative_sigma`. The coprime version `sigma_mul_coprime` follows from `isMultiplicative_sigma.map_mul_of_coprime h`. Together with the prime power formula, multiplicativity reduces computing σ(n) to computing σ at each prime power in n's factorization. Multiplicativity also means σ is determined by its Dirichlet series: σ(n) = Σ_{d|n} d = (id ∗ 1)(n), the Dirichlet convolution of the identity and constant-1 function.

title: σ(p^k) = Geometric Sum: The Building Block for All σ Values
content: For a prime power p^k, the divisors are exactly {1, p, p², ..., p^k}, giving σ(p^k) = Σ_{i=0}^k p^i = (p^(k+1)-1)/(p-1). The Lean proof uses `sigma_apply_prime_pow hp` (Mathlib) and simplifies with `congr 1; ext i; ring`. Combined with multiplicativity, this gives the complete formula: σ(n) = Π_i (p_i^(a_i+1)-1)/(p_i-1) for n = Π_i p_i^a_i. The k=1,2,3 specializations are proved by unfolding `Finset.sum_range_succ`.
mathContext:
$$\sigma(p^k) = 1 + p + p^2 + \cdots + p^k = \frac{p^{k+1}-1}{p-1}$$
General formula:
$$\sigma\!\left(\prod_i p_i^{a_i}\right) = \prod_i \frac{p_i^{a_i+1}-1}{p_i-1}$$

title: Module Overview: σ Properties and Classification in 14 Parts
content:
The module header documents a 14-part development of the sum of divisors function σ(n) = Σ_{d|n} d, building from concrete computed values through general structural theorems to historical and analytical connections. The file is organized pedagogically: Parts 1–2 establish empirical evidence (specific σ values), Parts 3–6 classify numbers and compute related functions, Parts 7–10 prove general bounds and connections, and Parts 11–14 develop the algebraic theory (multiplicativity, prime power formula, factorization computation, and minimality).

The mathematical foundation is Mathlib's `ArithmeticFunction.sigma`: `sigma k n = Σ_{d|n} d^k`. This file uses `sigma 1` (ordinary sum of divisors), `sigma 0` (divisor count d(n)), and `sigma 2` (sum of squared divisors). Opening both `Nat` and `ArithmeticFunction` gives access to divisor-theoretic APIs throughout.
mathContext: $\sigma_k(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d^k$. Special cases: $\sigma_0(n) = d(n)$ (divisor count), $\sigma_1(n) = \sigma(n)$ (sum of divisors), $\sigma_2(n)$ (sum of squared divisors). These are the first three members of the Dirichlet series family $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_k(n) n^{-s} = \zeta(s)\zeta(s-k)$.

title: Part 2: σ(p) = p+1 Verified for Six Specific Primes
content:
Before proving the general theorem, Part 2 verifies σ(p) = p+1 for the first six primes {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13} using `native_decide`. Each theorem is stated as `sigma 1 p = p + 1` in the form Lean uses for the general formula (matching the output of `sigma_apply_prime_pow`), making the transition to the general proof natural.

These specific verifications serve two purposes: they build intuition about why σ(p) = p+1 (the only divisors of a prime are 1 and p itself), and they provide immediately usable lemmas that the later factorization examples can reference directly without invoking the general theorem. The pattern also illustrates `native_decide` at its strongest — verifiable computation that would be tedious to prove by hand.
mathContext:
$p$ prime $\Rightarrow$ divisors$(p) = \{1, p\}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\sigma(p) = 1 + p$.
Verified: $\sigma(2) = 3, \sigma(3) = 4, \sigma(5) = 6, \sigma(7) = 8, \sigma(11) = 12, \sigma(13) = 14$.
All primes are deficient since $\sigma(p) = p + 1 < 2p$ for $p \geq 2$.

title: Abundancy Index: σ(n)/n as a Rational Characterization of Perfection
content:
The abundancy index `abundancy n = σ(n)/n : ℚ` is the ratio of the divisor sum to n itself. It provides a scale-independent measure of how 'divisor-rich' a number is: deficient numbers have abundancy < 2, perfect numbers have abundancy = 2, and abundant numbers have abundancy > 2.

The theorem `perfect_iff_abundancy_two` proves: n > 0 → (IsPerfect n ↔ abundancy n = 2). The proof uses `field_simp` and `exact_mod_cast` to work with the rational equation σ(n)/n = 2, then `omega` for the natural number arithmetic. The `noncomputable` annotation marks `abundancy` as using real division (rational, noncomputable in Lean's kernel).

The abundancy index appears naturally in the theory of perfect and amicable numbers: (m, n) is amicable iff σ(m)/m + σ(n)/n = ... Wait, more precisely: abundancy(m) = abundancy(n) = (m+n)/m when gcd(m,n)=1 is not necessarily required. The abundance index is used in the theory of quasi-perfect and multiperfect numbers (σ(n) = kn for integer k ≥ 2).
mathContext:
$$\text{abundancy}(n) = \frac{\sigma(n)}{n} \in \mathbb{Q}$$
Classification: deficient $\Leftrightarrow$ abundancy $< 2$, perfect $\Leftrightarrow$ abundancy $= 2$, abundant $\Leftrightarrow$ abundancy $> 2$.
For Mersenne perfect numbers: $\text{abundancy}(2^{p-1}(2^p-1)) = \frac{(2^p-1)(2^p)}{2^{p-1}(2^p-1)} = 2$.

title: Parts 7–8: Divisor Count d(n) and Sum of Squared Divisors σ₂
content:
Parts 7 and 8 compute two related arithmetic functions using the same `sigma k` infrastructure:

**Divisor count d(n) = σ₀(n)** (`sigma 0 n`): Counts the number of divisors. Key computed values: d(1)=1, d(2)=2, d(4)=3, d(6)=4, d(12)=6, d(1024)=11. Note d(2^10) = 11 = 10+1, which is the general formula d(p^k) = k+1 for prime powers. Highly composite numbers (1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, ...) maximize d(n) for their size — these are Ramanujan's highly composite numbers mentioned in Part 10.

**Sum of squared divisors σ₂(n)** (`sigma 2 n`): Key values: σ₂(1)=1, σ₂(2)=5, σ₂(6)=50. The general formula is σ₂(p^k) = (p^(2k+2)-1)/(p²-1). Both functions inherit multiplicativity from `isMultiplicative_sigma`.
mathContext:
$$d(n) = \sigma_0(n) = \sum_{d|n} 1, \quad \sigma_2(n) = \sum_{d|n} d^2$$
Dirichlet series: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d(n) n^{-s} = \zeta(s)^2$ and $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_2(n) n^{-s} = \zeta(s)\zeta(s-2)$.
For prime powers: $d(p^k) = k+1$, $\sigma_2(p^k) = 1 + p^2 + p^4 + \cdots + p^{2k} = \frac{p^{2k+2}-1}{p^2-1}$.

title: Part 9: σ(n) ≥ n for All n ≥ 1
content:
The basic lower bound `sigma_ge_self : ∀ n ≥ 1, σ(n) ≥ n` is proved by observing that n is always a divisor of itself, so the divisor sum includes n as one term. In Lean: n ∈ n.divisors (proved via `Nat.mem_divisors` with `n ∣ n` and `n ≠ 0`), then `Finset.single_le_sum` gives σ(n) = Σ_{d|n} d ≥ n.

This lower bound, combined with the strict inequality `sigma_gt_self : ∀ n > 1, σ(n) > n`, shows that every n > 1 is non-deficient-with-equality: n divides σ(n) - n (the aliquot sum) only when n = 1. The bound σ(n) ≥ n means perfect numbers satisfy σ(n) = 2n exactly at the minimum of the abundant side — no 'slack' exists.
mathContext:
$$\sigma(n) \geq n \quad (\text{since } n \in \{d : d \mid n\})$$
$$\sigma(n) > n \quad \text{for } n > 1 \quad (\text{since also } 1 \mid n, 1 \neq n)$$
These bounds are tight: $\sigma(1) = 1$ achieves equality in the first, and no $n > 1$ achieves equality in the second (that would require divisors$(n) = \{n\}$, impossible since $1 \mid n$).

title: Part 10: Robin's Inequality, Gronwall's Theorem, and the RH Connection
content:
Part 10 is a commentary section (no Lean proofs) documenting three deep connections of σ to advanced mathematics:

**Robin's Inequality (1984)**: σ(n) < e^γ · n · ln(ln(n)) for all n > 5040, where γ ≈ 0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. Remarkably, Robin proved this is *equivalent* to the Riemann Hypothesis. The threshold 5040 = 7! is special: σ(5040)/5040 is one of the largest known values of σ(n)/n, and verifying Robin's inequality for n ≤ 5040 by computation leaves the infinite tail equivalent to RH.

**Gronwall's Theorem (1913)**: lim sup_{n→∞} σ(n)/(n ln(ln(n))) = e^γ ≈ 1.7811. This shows the bound in Robin's inequality is tight — not improvable by a constant factor.

**Ramanujan's Highly Composite Numbers**: Numbers where d(n) > d(m) for all m < n (sequence 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 36, ...) maximize both d(n) and, often, σ(n)/n. These are the 'opposite extreme' from primes — maximally composite rather than minimally composite.
mathContext:
**Robin's inequality** (equivalent to RH): $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma n \ln\!\ln n$ for all $n > 5040$.
**Gronwall**: $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\sigma(n)}{n \ln\!\ln n} = e^\gamma$.
**Dirichlet series**: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\sigma(n)}{n^s} = \zeta(s)\zeta(s-1)$, convergent for $\Re(s) > 2$.

title: Part 13: Computing σ via Prime Factorization
content:
Parts 12–13 demonstrate the full algorithmic power of multiplicativity + the prime power formula: given any n = p₁^a₁ · p₂^a₂ · ... · pₖ^aₖ, compute σ(n) = σ(p₁^a₁) · ... · σ(pₖ^aₖ) = Π_i (Σ_{j=0}^{a_i} p_i^j).

Two explicit examples:
- **σ(12)**: 12 = 2² · 3, so σ(12) = σ(4) · σ(3) = (1+2+4) · (1+3) = 7 · 4 = 28. The Lean proof `sigma_twelve_via_factorization` writes this as `sigma 1 12 = (1+2+2²) · (1+3)` and uses `rw [h12, sigma_mul_coprime, sigma_prime_pow_two, sigma_prime]` for the Coprime(4,3) factorization.

- **σ(30)**: 30 = 2 · 3 · 5, so σ(30) = σ(2) · σ(3) · σ(5) = 3 · 4 · 6 = 72. The proof applies `sigma_mul_coprime` twice — first for (2, 15), then for (3, 5) — and invokes `sigma_prime` for each factor.

These examples show that σ is entirely computable from the prime factorization, reducing σ for any n (however large) to evaluating geometric sums at each prime power.

title: Part 14: 12 is the Smallest Abundant Number — Minimality via interval_cases
content:
The minimality proof that 12 is the smallest abundant number uses two complementary results:

1. **`not_abundant_lt_12`**: For every n with 0 < n < 12, ¬IsAbundant n. The proof uses `interval_cases n`, which case-splits on n ∈ {1,...,11} and generates 11 subgoals, each closed by `simp_all` and `native_decide`. This is the standard Lean pattern for exhaustive minimality proofs over small integer ranges.

2. **`twelve_smallest_abundant`**: Combines `twelve_is_abundant` (from Part 3) with `not_abundant_lt_12` into the final theorem: IsAbundant 12 ∧ ∀ n, 0 < n → n < 12 → ¬IsAbundant n.

Historically, 12 = 2² · 3 is the smallest number with σ(12) = 28 > 24 = 2·12. The next abundant numbers are 18, 20, 24 — all even. The smallest odd abundant number is 945 = 3³ · 5 · 7, discovered in the Middle Ages and not provably minimal until modern computer verification. The formalization here for n < 12 uses exactly 11 native_decide calls, illustrating how verification replaces open-ended search for small bounds.
mathContext:
$$12 = 2^2 \cdot 3: \quad \sigma(12) = (1+2+4)(1+3) = 28 > 24 = 2 \cdot 12$$
For $n \in \{1,\ldots,11\}$: the deficient values are $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11$ ($\sigma(n) < 2n$) and perfect value is $6$ ($\sigma(6)=12=2\cdot 6$). No abundant values exist below 12.
Smallest odd abundant: $\sigma(945) = \sigma(3^3)\sigma(5)\sigma(7) = 40 \cdot 6 \cdot 8 = 1920 > 1890 = 2 \cdot 945$.
